extracted.intended_audience: Patent Examining Corps / USPTO patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: USPTO memorandum instructing patent examiners how to apply 35 U.S.C. § 101 to nucleic-acid-related claims in light of the Supreme Court's decision in Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics, Inc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturally occurring nucleic acids not patent eligible merely because isolated
rubrics_metrics.description: As of today, naturally occurring nucleic acids are not patent eligible merely because they have been isolated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should now reject product claims drawn solely to naturally occurring nucleic acids or fragments thereof, whether isolated or not, as being ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to non-naturally-occurring nucleic acids may be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims clearly limited to non-naturally-occurring nucleic acids, such as a cDNA or a nucleic acid in which the order of the naturally-occurring nucleotides has been altered (e.g., a man-made variant sequence), remain eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court held that 'cDNA is not a 'product of nature' and is patent eligible under § 101.' Use this distinction when assessing composition claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation of a gene is not an act of invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court held that isolating a 'gene from its surrounding genetic material is not an act of invention.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Isolation alone—removing a gene from its natural context—does not convert a naturally occurring gene into patent-eligible subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method and other claims involving naturally occurring nucleic acids require careful § 101 analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Other claims, including method claims, that involve naturally occurring nucleic acids may give rise to eligibility issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims should be examined under the existing guidance in MPEP 2106, Patent Subject Matter Eligibility, to determine whether they present eligibility problems under § 101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supreme Court's factual holding on 'product of nature' for isolated DNA
rubrics_metrics.description: In Myriad, the Supreme Court held that certain claims to isolated DNA are not patent-eligible, because they read on isolated naturally-occurring DNA that is a 'product of nature.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Court's analysis distinguishing natural products from man-made compositions when determining eligibility; claims that 'read on' a product of nature should be treated as ineligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO to issue further comprehensive guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO is closely reviewing the decision in Myriad and will issue more comprehensive guidance on patent subject matter eligibility determinations, including the role isolation plays in those determinations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat this memorandum as preliminary guidance; examiners should follow this direction now but expect updated, more detailed instructions in forthcoming USPTO guidance.
